analysis.one_liner: Lets shooting victims sue handgun and assault weapon makers and dealers for damages.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and its Crime Subcommittee and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let anyone hurt or killed by a handgun or assault weapon sue the manufacturer, importer, or dealer in federal court. The gun companies would be responsible for damages automatically, with no need to prove the gun was defective or the seller did anything wrong. It would not apply to injuries to people committing felonies, self-inflicted injuries, or shootings by police or soldiers on duty.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of handgun and assault weapon shootings and their families, who could win compensation for medical bills, lost income, and death without proving the gun industry did anything negligent.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of gun shootings and their families

how_it_helps.text: Any person injured or killed by a handgun or assault weapon could sue the gun's manufacturer, importer, or dealer in federal court for damages.
Defendants would be strictly liable, meaning victims would not have to prove fault or a defective product, only that the gun fired and hurt them.
Courts could award attorney's fees to the prevailing party, making it easier for ordinary victims to afford to sue.

analysis.who_pays: Gun manufacturers, importers, and dealers, who would owe damages for shooting injuries involving guns they made or sold after the law took effect, and would likely pass much of that cost into gun prices.

drawbacks.text: Because liability applies without proof of any defect or wrongdoing, a dealer who legally sold a gun to a licensed buyer could still owe damages if that gun were later used to shoot someone, a cost that could drive some dealers out of business or sharply raise gun prices.

The bill applies only to handguns and assault weapons, and excludes injuries to people committing felonies, self-inflicted injuries, and police or military shootings, so many shooting victims would get no remedy under it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give shooting victims a new way to recover real damages and shift the cost of gun violence to the industry that profits from the guns. The tradeoff is that strict liability with no fault requirement would put enormous potential costs on sellers of perfectly legal products, likely raising prices or shrinking availability. How that cost would be shared between the industry and buyers was never tested because the bill never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its Crime Subcommittee for the rest of the Congress and was never brought to a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Cardiss Collins of Illinois introduced the bill on January 27, 1993.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on January 27, 1993.
On February 10, 1993, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice, where no further action was recorded.
Only two additional members, Representatives Gutierrez and Serrano, signed on as cosponsors, and the bill never reached the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers, importers, and dealers, who avoided strict liability for shooting damages, and no one else gained anything because the bill simply died.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The gun industry, which faced no new liability

for.name: Rep. Cardiss Collins
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and promoted it in floor remarks on three occasions.

for.name: Reps. Luis Gutierrez and Jose Serrano
for.what_they_did: Added their names as cosponsors in July 1993.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Democrat in the 103rd Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 27, 1993, sent it to its Crime Subcommittee, and never reported it out or scheduled any vote.

against.name: House Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from February 10, 1993 onward with no hearings or action recorded.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats, and no Republican support is recorded; the bill never advanced beyond committee.

industries.note: The bill would have made them automatically liable for damages whenever a handgun or assault weapon they made or sold after enactment was fired and hurt someone. Their interest in killing the bill ran directly against shooting victims who would have gained a new source of compensation.
